title: Game Developer
summary: Game developers write the code that makes games play: movement, physics, AI, UI and tools, usually inside an engine like Unity or Godot. It suits students who like programming, maths and finishing small playable things.

nodes.title: Programming in C#
nodes.summary: Learn one language well: variables, loops, functions, classes and collections. C# is used for Unity scripting and is also supported by Godot, so it is a practical first choice.

resources.title: Get started with C#, Part 1 – Microsoft Learn

nodes.proof: A console game (such as number guessing or tic-tac-toe) in C# with classes and clean, commented code on GitHub.

nodes.title: Maths for games
nodes.summary: Vectors, matrices and coordinate systems are how games move, rotate and draw things. Revise linear algebra with a focus on what it means in 2D and 3D space rather than exam tricks.
nodes.proof: A small script or demo that moves and rotates a shape using vector and matrix maths you wrote yourself.

nodes.title: A game engine: Unity or Godot
nodes.summary: Pick one engine and learn its editor, scenes, objects, physics, audio and scripting. Unity Essentials and Godot's step-by-step guide are free and aimed at beginners.
nodes.proof: Finish the Unity Essentials pathway or Godot's step-by-step section and show one scene you built yourself.

nodes.title: Build your first 2D games
nodes.summary: Make small, complete 2D games before anything big. Godot's 'Dodge the Creeps' tutorial covers player movement, enemies, score and UI; CS50's archived 2D course rebuilds classics like Pong and Breakout.
nodes.proof: Two small finished 2D games with a start screen, score and game-over, playable from a link.

nodes.title: Game code architecture
nodes.summary: As games grow, messy code slows you down. Learn common patterns such as component and observer, explained with examples in the free online book Game Programming Patterns.
nodes.proof: Refactor one of your games to use a state machine or component pattern and explain the change in the README.

nodes.title: Graphics fundamentals (optional)
nodes.summary: For engine or graphics roles, learn how a GPU draws a frame: vertex and fragment shaders, buffers and textures. LearnOpenGL teaches this in C++ with modern OpenGL.
nodes.proof: A C++ OpenGL program that draws a textured, rotating cube with your own shaders.

nodes.title: Join game jams
nodes.summary: Game jams are short events where you build a game around a theme, alone or in a team. itch.io lists many free online jams. They teach you to scope small, finish on time and work with others.
nodes.proof: Submit a playable entry to at least one online game jam and note what you would change after reading player feedback.

nodes.title: One polished portfolio game
nodes.summary: Take your best jam or practice game and polish it: menus, sound, juice, bug fixes and a short trailer or GIF. One finished, polished game usually says more than many half-built ones.
nodes.proof: A public game page with a playable build, screenshots, controls and a link to clean source code.

nodes.title: Interview prep and job search
nodes.summary: Prepare to explain your games' code, patterns and maths, and revise data structures and C# or C++ basics. Apply to game studios and also to related roles (simulation, AR/VR, interactive apps) that use the same engines.
nodes.proof: A one-page portfolio site linking your games, plus a mock interview where you walk through one system you built.
